title: Colleagues Who Don’t Pull Their Weight
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece addresses the frustration of working alongside colleagues who do less but share equally in credit and rewards. It first rules out the two instinctive responses: complaining to the team leader, which makes the complainer look like a whiner incapable of managing relationships, and confronting the colleague directly, which tends to freeze communication in protracted conflict. The article then makes a counterintuitive move, recommending that the frustrated colleague take on more of the slacker's work rather than less. By steadily removing tasks until the underperformer has nothing to do, the team makes their irrelevance visible to everyone, including leaders who check in. The piece argues that this exposure, rather than accusation, is what prompts most shirkers to seek assignments, while those who do not may lose their jobs.
points: Escalating a slacking colleague to the team leader tends to backfire, because the leader reads the complaint as evidence that the complainer cannot manage relationships or build a supportive climate.
Direct confrontation is framed as equally risky, since it often produces a protracted conflict in which communication stops altogether.
The recommended tactic is to absorb the underperformer's tasks until they have nothing left to do, making their uninvolvement visible without anyone having to accuse them.
Once exposed as irrelevant, most underperformers begin asking for work, and those who do not risk losing their positions.
quotes: Colleagues who don’t pull their weight miss deadlines, make mistakes, and stay out of sight when the hard work is getting done. Yet, they often get the same credit as everyone who put their shoulder into it. This can be both infuriating and demotivating.

Complaining to the team or project leader is a surefire way of looking like a crybaby and a whiner. The leader immediately believes you are incapable of managing relationships and creating a supportive climate.

You read that right. The key is to keep taking tasks and responsibilities away from them until they have nothing to do. At first, they happily sit on the sidelines and watch you and the team work for them.
It quickly becomes painfully obvious they are completely uninvolved and unimportant. Everyone around them sees them not only as a slacker, but as irrelevant.

Now fully exposed, most colleagues who don’t do their fair share of the work begin to clamor for assignments. With luck, they will lose their slothful ways and pick up a shovel. Those who don’t will sometimes find themselves without a job.
